2	name: code-review
3	description: Expert code review of the current branch diff and every staged, unstaged, and untracked file. Invoke before every commit, and again after any change to the reviewed state. Read-only — reports findings and an explicit approve/request-changes verdict, never edits files.
4	tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob
5	---
6	
7	You are an expert reviewer of the languages and frameworks used by this
8	application: C (C17), CMake, and classic terminal/CLI game programming. You
9	review the complete pending state of the worktree before it is committed.
10	
11	## Scope
12	
13	Review all of:
14	
15	- the branch diff against `main` (`git diff main...HEAD`),
16	- staged changes (`git diff --cached`),
17	- unstaged changes (`git diff`),
18	- untracked files (`git status --porcelain`, then read them).
19	
20	Read enough of the surrounding code (`sst.h`, callers, related modules) to
21	judge each change in context, not just the diff hunks.
22	
23	## What to look for
24	
25	- **Correctness**: logic errors, off-by-one errors, broken game rules, and
26	  behavior that contradicts `sst.doc` or the change's stated intent.
27	- **C-specific defects**: undefined behavior, out-of-bounds indexing, signed
28	  overflow, uninitialized reads, format-string mismatches, unchecked returns,
29	  memory and resource leaks, unsafe string handling (`strcpy`/`sprintf`
30	  without bounds).
31	- **Global state**: this codebase uses shared game state in `sst.h`; verify
32	  new code initializes, saves, and restores it consistently (snapshots,
33	  events, scoring).
34	- **Consistency**: naming, formatting, comment density, and idiom match the
35	  surrounding code; CMake changes follow the existing style and keep the
36	  feature flags (`SCORE`, `CAPTURE`, `CLOAKING`) working.
37	- **Scope hygiene**: accidental files, debug leftovers, unrelated edits, or
38	  changes that belong in a different branch.
39	- **Tests and docs**: tests match the behavior they claim to cover;
40	  player-visible changes are reflected in `sst.doc`/README when relevant.
41	- **Review coverage**: whether the diff can alter what the game shows a
42	  player or asks of them, and if it can, whether `ui-review` ran *on this
43	  state*. See "The review sub-agents" in `AGENTS.md` for what counts as
44	  reaching the player; unclear means the pass was owed. Read that from the
45	  file in the repository rather than from any copy already in context,
46	  which may predate the rule.
47	
48	  The author is required to tell you which passes ran, whether the last
49	  `ui-review` round saw the state being committed, and why any was
50	  skipped. Weigh that against the diff rather than accepting it, and say
51	  so when no claim was made at all — that leaves the question unanswered
52	  rather than answered in the author's favor. "It ran" is not enough on
53	  its own: ask for that pass's verdict and the list of what it says it
54	  exercised, which you can check against the diff. A run whose coverage
55	  names journeys the change cannot reach is worth as little as no run.
56	
57	  A change that reaches the player with none of that behind it is a
58	  blocker where the diff plainly reaches them and a should-fix where it
59	  is arguable — not a nit either way. You read code, that pass reads
60	  screens, and neither substitutes for the other. The skip is the
61	  author's own judgment about their own work, and you are the pass
62	  positioned to dispute it before the commit exists.
63	
64	Report only real, actionable findings. Do not pad the review with
65	observations that would not change what the author does next.
66	
67	## Output
68	
69	Do not modify any files. Report:
70	
71	1. **Verdict**: approve, or request changes. Approval is only valid for the
72	   exact state you reviewed — note the commit and a summary of the pending
73	   changes it covers.
74	2. **Findings**, ordered by severity (blocker / should-fix / nit), each with
75	   `file:line`, a one-sentence statement of the defect, the concrete failure
76	   scenario, and a suggested fix.
77	3. Anything you could not review and why.
78

2	name: ui-review
3	description: Reviews the user-facing behavior of the Super Star Trek CLI game. Acts as an expert in games and CLI games. Invoke after an implementation pass when the change can alter what the game shows a player or asks of them, before running the verifier, and again after any fix that changes what a player sees. See "The review sub-agents" in AGENTS.md for when this binds; when it is unclear, run it. Read-only — reports findings, never edits files.
4	tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob
5	---
6	
7	You are an expert reviewer of games and CLI games, with deep familiarity with
8	classic terminal games such as the original Super Star Trek. You review the
9	user-facing behavior of the change currently on this branch.
10	
11	## Scope
12	
13	Review the player-visible surface of the current change: what the game shows
14	a player, or asks of them.
15	
16	Which changes reach a player is decided in `AGENTS.md`, under "The review
17	sub-agents" — it draws the line, names the cases either way, including ones
18	that look internal and reach the player anyway, and says to run this pass
19	where the answer is unclear. Read it there, from the file in the repository
20	rather than from any copy already in context, which may predate the rule.
21	A second copy of that list living here is the drift this file was brought
22	back into step to fix.
23	
24	What is left out is surface that the game never shows anyone playing it —
25	where the only effect is on somebody building or operating it.
26	
27	Determine what changed by inspecting the branch diff against `main` plus all
28	staged, unstaged, and untracked files, then evaluate how those changes look
29	and feel to a player.
30	
31	## How to review
32	
33	1. Read the diff to understand which commands, prompts, messages, or screens
34	   are affected.
35	2. Build the game if needed (`cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug &&
36	   cmake --build build`) and drive the affected behavior through
37	   `./build/sst`, scripting input via a pipe or heredoc when interactive play
38	   is impractical.
39	3. Consult `sst.doc` and the README so your judgment matches the game's
40	   documented behavior and the conventions of the original game.
41	
42	## What to evaluate
43	
44	- **Clarity**: prompts, command feedback, and error messages are unambiguous
45	  and tell the player what to do next.
46	- **Consistency**: wording, capitalization, spacing, and table/grid alignment
47	  match the rest of the game's output; new commands follow existing
48	  abbreviation and prompting conventions.
49	- **Game feel**: pacing, flavor text, and tone fit a classic Star Trek CLI
50	  game; information the player needs for a decision is available when the
51	  decision is asked for.
52	- **Discoverability**: new or changed behavior is reachable through help,
53	  command lists, or documentation (`sst.doc`).
54	- **Terminal correctness**: output renders sensibly in a plain 80-column
55	  terminal; no garbled control sequences, truncated lines, or misaligned
56	  charts.
57	- **Regressions**: existing journeys (starting a game, moving, combat,
58	  docking, reports, ending a game) still behave and read correctly where the
59	  change could plausibly affect them.
60	
61	## Output
62	
63	Do not modify any files. Report:
64	
65	1. A one-paragraph verdict: acceptable as-is, or needs changes.
66	2. Actionable findings, each with severity (blocker / should-fix / nit), the
67	   affected file and behavior, what a player experiences, and a concrete
68	   suggestion.
69	3. What you actually exercised (commands run, journeys played) so the main
70	   agent knows the coverage of this review.
71

1	# AGENTS.md
2	
3	Shared instructions for every coding agent working in this repository
4	(Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, and others). `CLAUDE.md` imports this
5	file; keep all rules here so every agent sees the same thing.
6	
7	## Project
8	
9	Super Star Trek — a classic terminal (CLI) space strategy game written in C17,
10	built with CMake. The executable is `sst`. Game documentation lives in
11	`sst.doc`; shared declarations live in `sst.h`.
12	
13	Global game state uses the `EXTERN`/`INCLUDED` trick in `sst.h`: exactly one
14	translation unit per binary defines `INCLUDED` before including `sst.h` to
15	instantiate the globals (`sst.c` for the game; a test's own file, e.g.
16	`tests/test_tuifmt.c`, for test binaries that don't link `sst.c`).
17	
18	Display state (`tui_active`, `tui_ingame`) deliberately sits outside that
19	mechanism — plain `extern` in `tui.h`, defined in `tui.c` — so `tui.h`
20	stays self-contained for `osx.c`, which cannot include `sst.h`. Put new
21	display flags there, not in `sst.h`.
22	
23	`osx.c` is the file that cannot include `sst.h`: `sst.h` declares
24	`pause(int)`, which collides with the POSIX `pause(void)` that `osx.c`
25	needs. So what `osx.c` *provides* is declared in `osx.h` (included by
26	both `osx.c` and `sst.h`), and what `osx.c` *calls* it gets from
27	`tui.h`. Put new platform functions in `osx.h`, not `sst.h`, so the
28	definition stays checked against the declaration — `-Wmissing-prototypes`
29	is on and CI builds with `-Werror`.
30	
31	## Build and run
32	
33	```sh
34	cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug   # build type is required; Debug adds -DDEBUG
35	cmake --build build
36	./build/sst
37	```
38	
39	Note: `CMakeLists.txt` compares `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` directly, so configuring
40	without `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=...` fails. `-Wall -Wextra` is always on; CI
41	also configures with `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, so pass that locally to see what
42	CI will refuse. Feature flags `-DSCORE -DCAPTURE
43	-DCLOAKING` are always enabled.
44	
45	## TUI mode (`sst -t`)
46	
47	- All game output must go through `prout`/`proutn`/`proutf`/`prouts` and all
48	  input through `scan()`/`getch()`/`readinput()` — raw `printf`/`putchar`/
49	  `fgets` silently bypasses the full-screen mode.
50	- Plain mode (no `-t`) must not change as an unintended side effect of any
51	  change; verify with a piped scripted journey (e.g.
52	  `printf 'regular\nshort\nnovice\nxyz\nsrscan\nquit\nn\n' | ./build/sst`).
53	  If a change alters plain-mode output on purpose, say so in the commit
54	  and explain why.
55	- Text the game prints must not end in a carriage return. `sst.doc` is
56	  CRLF, so anything read from it needs both stripped: under curses a
57	  trailing `\r` returns the cursor to column 0 and the newline then
58	  erases the line. `pause()` writes a CR deliberately, to wipe its own
59	  prompt in place -- the one exception, and the reason the test scripts
60	  filter that shape before checking.
61	- The panel formatters in `tuifmt.c` must mirror `srscan()` in `reports.c`
62	  exactly — it is the spec, including sensor-damage masking and the `-f`
63	  coordinate transposition (x is the column). Keep `tests/test_tuifmt.c` in
64	  sync (`ctest --test-dir build -R '^tuifmt$'`).
65	- Testing the TUI needs a pty: use tmux, and always on your own socket via
66	  `-L`, with `-f /dev/null` so the config does not follow — `tmux -f /dev/null
67	  -L sst new-session -d -x 100 -y 30 -s t './build/sst -t; sleep 30'`, drive
68	  with `tmux -f /dev/null -L sst send-keys -t t 'cmd' Enter` (input is
69	  line-based; keys need Enter), inspect with `capture-pane -t t -p`, and clean
70	  up with `kill-server` on that same socket. Without `-f /dev/null` a setting
71	  as ordinary as `base-index 1` renames the pane out from under you and every
72	  capture comes back empty. The default socket is where the
73	  human running you keeps their own work: on 2026-08-01 a review agent tidied up
74	  after a TUI check with a bare `tmux kill-server` and destroyed a week-old
75	  session of eight panes, including the agent's own parent. `-L` is what makes
76	  that mistake impossible rather than merely discouraged — never issue a bare
77	  `tmux kill-server`, and never `kill-session` a session you did not create.
78	  Never redirect the game's stdout in the session — it breaks curses rendering.
79	  `tests/tui.sh` does all of this automatically and is the place to add
80	  coverage; it skips without tmux, but fails rather than skipping when `$CI` is
81	  set.
82	- Check the TUI at 80x24 and 72x24, not just at a comfortable size. 72x24 is
83	  the smallest it accepts and 80x24 is what most terminals open at; the
84	  message window is only ten lines at both, which is where the paging bugs
85	  live.
86	
87	## The golden recordings
88	
89	A failing `golden` test means a journey's output changed. Work out why
90	and say so in the commit -- the fixture diff is the evidence a reviewer
91	needs. Never re-record with `tests/golden.sh <sst> --update` to turn CI
92	green without that explanation; the recordings are the only thing in
93	the suite that checks the game's arithmetic at all.
94	
95	## Development workflow
96	
97	Every coding agent working in this repository must follow this workflow.
98	
99	1. **Inspect before changing anything.** Inspect the repository, current Git
100	   state, all applicable instruction files, and the issue or roadmap item the
101	   work comes from, before making changes. Preserve unrelated staged,
102	   unstaged, and untracked work.
103	
104	2. **Create a branch first.** Create a dedicated feature, fix, refactor, chore,
105	   test, or documentation branch before making code changes. Never commit
106	   directly to `main`, and create the branch from the latest appropriate
107	   `main` state.
108	
109	3. **Choose a thin vertical slice.** Before implementing a roadmap item or
110	   feature, define the smallest end-to-end slice that can be reviewed, tested,
111	   shipped, and merged independently. Prefer one coherent user-visible or
112	   operational outcome over a broad horizontal layer.
113	
114	   The slice inherits whatever the issue assumes, so check what it claims
115	   before building on it. A claim you can settle — what the code does, what
116	   `sst.doc` says at a given line — you settle, and where it does not hold
117	   you say so on the issue in a comment: what it claimed, what is actually
118	   the case, and the line that shows it. Comment, do not rewrite the issue
119	   body; a comment keeps straight who said what. A closed issue still
120	   takes one, and an issue closed by the pull request that got the premise
121	   wrong is exactly where the correction belongs. Where you cannot comment
122	   at all — a locked issue, a harness with no access to the tracker — say
123	   it in the pull request body and the summary of the work, marked as
124	   unposted.
125	
126	   What is worth building stays the issue author's judgment. A wrong premise
127	   voids the claim it supports, not the issue, and the acceptance criteria
128	   it never touched still bind. Where the facts change what the issue
129	   ought to ask for, say so and ask — do not swap in a slice of your own.
130	   Say what was wrong and what the correction changed about the slice, in
131	   the pull request body and in the summary of the work, in the summary
132	   alone when there is no pull request. Silence is worse than either:
133	   building on a mistake you have seen, or building something else and
134	   leaving the issue describing work nobody did.
135	
136	   #58 is the example, and it reasoned well from one wrong fact. On its
137	   main ground it ruled out checking the galaxy's digit packing because
138	   that packing "appears nowhere in `sst.doc`" — where the manual gives it
139	   at `sst.doc:436-439`, as the meaning of the long-range scan. The
140	   instinct was the one step 4 now endorses, to take an expectation from
141	   somewhere independent of the code; only the fact about where that
142	   source was silent was wrong. It cost a narrower slice than the facts
143	   allowed, not the wrong one.
144	
145	4. **Use test-driven development when behavior or structure is testable.**
146	   - Add or update a focused test before implementation.
147	   - Run it and confirm it fails for the expected reason.
148	   - Implement the smallest appropriate change.
149	   - Run focused tests while iterating.
150	   - Refactor only while the relevant tests remain green.
151	
152	   Run that loop yourself rather than delegating it. "Who runs which
153	   tests" after this list says why, and which tests belong to the
154	   `verifier` instead.
155	
156	   A test written against behavior that already exists — a recording, a
157	   check of something the game has always done — never has that failing
158	   first run to show for itself, and that is where tests which assert
159	   nothing come from. Prove it can fail some other way.
160	
161	   - Break what it checks, watch the test report it, and write down what
162	     was broken both in the commit and in a comment beside the assertion.
163	     The commit is invisible to whoever next edits the test.
164	   - Where the test compares against a literal in its own file, changing
165	     the literal proves it in a second. What follows is for tests that run
166	     the whole game and read what it printed.
167	   - Break it outside the repository. Copy the working tree — the current
168	     one, uncommitted test and all — somewhere else, leave `build/`
169	     behind, and configure a fresh one there: a copied `build/` still
170	     names the original source directory in its cache, so building in the
171	     copy compiles the original's sources — your break never reaches the
172	     binary, and the test passes for the wrong reason. It prints a
173	     cache-path error and exits 0 while it does it, and a regeneration
174	     can rewrite the original's build files on the way past. Most tests
175	     here take the binary as an argument. Run from inside the copy:
176	     `cd <copy> && tests/tournament.sh build/sst Debug`, or `ctest
177	     --test-dir build -R '^(tuifmt|rules)$'` for the two compiled ones.
178	     From inside, because for some of them the script decides which tree
179	     is read and not the binary: `help` and `tui` find `sst.doc` from
180	     their own path, and `golden` its fixtures. The original's script
181	     pointed at the copy's binary proves the original's data and comes
182	     back green — the same wrong-reason pass as the stale `build/`
183	     above. The two that read the tree instead, `instructions` and
184	     `score`, take `.` from in there. A `git worktree` will not do: it
185	     holds `HEAD`, not the test you have just written.
186	   - Break the game, not the test — and break it somewhere the test's
187	     expectation does not come from. A break that both sides of the
188	     comparison descend from cancels out: setup writes the galaxy word
189	     wrong, the code that reads it back fills the quadrant to match, both
190	     scans agree, and nothing moves. Rounding, clamping and sensor masking
191	     swallow a break the same way. Prefer a path where the expected value
192	     comes from somewhere independent — `sst.doc`, a literal, a subsystem
193	     that does not share the representation.
194	   - A green run means one of two things: the test is blind, or the break
195	     was. Rule out the second before touching the test.
196	   - This proof, unlike the loop above, is one a sub-agent can run for you.
197	     "Who runs which tests" says when that is worth doing, and what the
198	     sub-agent has to report back for the record this asks you to keep.
199	   - Where a test reaches its subject only on some of the data it runs
200	     over — one seed, one galaxy, one game that happened to dock — assert
201	     that the case it needs really occurred. Otherwise the day the data
202	     stops providing it, the test keeps passing and says nothing.
203	
204	   Three assertions in #64 passed against builds that broke them: one
205	   counted rows from scans it was not looking at, one searched for a line
206	   the game does not print at the skill it ran at, and one multiplied a
207	   term that was zero in every galaxy the battery then played — a seed
208	   whose opening quadrant holds a starbase had to be added before that
209	   assertion meant anything. All three read convincingly.
210	
211	5. **Inspect the complete diff.** Review the branch diff plus all staged,
212	   unstaged, and untracked files. Remove accidental or unrelated changes while
213	   preserving work that belongs to the user. What you drop because it was
214	   unrelated is often worth filing; see step 9.
215	
216	6. **Run `ui-review` before verification.** After the main agent completes an
217	   implementation pass, invoke the `ui-review` sub-agent whenever the change
218	   can alter what the game shows a player or asks of them. The `ui-review`
219	   sub-agent must act as an expert in games and CLI games. Fix every
220	   actionable finding, or resolve it explicitly, before moving on — the
221	   standard that "Answering a finding" below sets for all three passes.
222	   If fixing one changes what the game shows a player, rerun `ui-review`
223	   on the result: the fixes made for #46 introduced a doubled echo, a
224	   duplicated question, a line cut mid-word and a cursor left where the
225	   next keystroke typed over the answer, each of them found by a later
226	   round rather than by the one that caused it. Read "The review
227	   sub-agents" after this list for when this pass binds, what to say when
228	   it does not, and — if you are not Claude Code — how to get any of
229	   these three passes at all.
230	
231	7. **Run `verifier` before code review.** Invoke the `verifier` sub-agent to
232	   run the builds, static checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for
233	   the change. The verifier must report failures, flakes, missing coverage,
234	   and environment issues. Fix every actionable finding, or resolve it
235	   explicitly, before starting code review. If a verifier finding requires a
236	   code change, rerun the verifier after addressing it.
237	
238	   The battery is the `verifier`'s work and not the main agent's, which
239	   is what "Who runs which tests" after this list is about.
240	
241	8. **Run `code-review` before every commit.** Invoke the `code-review`
242	   sub-agent against the current branch diff and every staged, unstaged, and
243	   untracked file. The reviewer must act as an expert in the languages and
244	   frameworks used by this application. Fix every actionable finding, or
245	   resolve it explicitly, before committing. If review findings cause changes,
246	   rerun the appropriate tests and the `verifier`, then obtain a fresh
247	   `code-review` approval for the changed state.
248	
249	   Tell it which of the passes above ran, whether the last `ui-review`
250	   round saw the state being committed, and where `ui-review` did not
251	   run, why. The middle one is what makes the rerun rule in step 6
252	   auditable: a fix made after that pass reported is a change it never
253	   saw, and "it ran" is a true answer that hides it.
254	
255	   The skip itself is the author's judgment about the author's own
256	   change — unlike the `verifier`'s scope, which the `verifier` decides
257	   and reports for itself. `code-review` binds on every commit whatever the
258	   change touched, so it is the pass certain to see the claim, and to be
259	   able to dispute it while the work can still change. Left to the commit
260	   and the pull request, the decision reaches a reader only once the work
261	   is finished, which is disclosure rather than review.
262	
263	9. **File what you found outside the slice.** Work turns up problems that
264	   belong to no slice in particular: a defect the change did not cause, a
265	   test that cannot fail, a comment that is no longer true. Open a GitHub
266	   issue for each as you find it, without waiting to be asked — a finding
267	   that lives only in a session summary is a finding nobody will act on.
268	   Standing here at step 9 makes this the last check that nothing was left
269	   unfiled, not the moment to begin. The main agent files them; the review
270	   sub-agents only report.
271	
272	   - Search the open issues first. If it is already filed, add what you
273	     learned to that issue instead of opening a second one.
274	   - File a real defect — anything that would mislead a player or a
275	     maintainer — and a coverage gap, meaning a test that cannot fail or
276	     that asserts less than it appears to. Leave style preferences and
277	     speculative ideas out; they belong in the pull request body. When it
278	     is genuinely unclear, file it: a wrong issue costs one close.
279	   - **Do not fix it in this slice.** An unrelated fix buried in an
280	     unrelated diff is how both the fix and the finding go unreviewed. Fix
281	     it here only if it belongs to the slice.
282	   - That is not license to file what steps 3, 4 and 6-8 require you to
283	     fix. A premise the slice rests on is corrected under step 3, not
284	     deferred; a test of your own that cannot fail is fixed under step 4. A
285	     `ui-review`, `verifier` or `code-review` finding about *this* change is
286	     resolved here; filing it is not resolving it. What gets filed is what
287	     those reviews turn up about code the change did not touch, and
288	     whatever you meet while reading for some other purpose.
289	   - Give the issue what the next person needs: what is wrong, why it
290	     matters, where it was found, and how to see it, citing `sst.doc` or a
291	     file and line where one applies.
292	   - Where the work depends on the unfixed behavior, name the issue in a
293	     comment beside it. Write that comment as part of the implementation,
294	     so it reaches the reviewer rather than arriving after approval.
295	   - Say which issues were filed, in the pull request body and in the
296	     summary of the work — in the summary alone when there is no pull
297	     request. An agent that cannot open issues says so plainly and lists
298	     the findings in the same places, marked as unfiled, so a human can
299	     file them. Silence is the one outcome this step exists to prevent.
300	
301	10. **Commit once the passes are answered.** Commit only after verification
302	    and code review are complete, with every finding answered — a finding
303	    resolved rather than fixed needs no fresh approval, which is why this
304	    does not say "after approval". Use Conventional Commits:
305	
306	    ```text
307	    <type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>
308	    ```
309	
310	    Keep the subject at 72 characters or fewer, describe why in the body when
311	    useful, and do not combine unrelated work.
312	
313	11. **Create pull requests from the reviewed state.**
314	    - Confirm that local verification remains valid.
315	    - Rerun `code-review` only if the reviewed state changed after the
316	      pre-commit review. A changed state includes code, tests,
317	      documentation, generated files, conflict resolution, or any other
318	      staged, unstaged, or untracked content.
319	    - Do not repeat code review when the already-reviewed diff and
320	      worktree remain unchanged. The `verifier` follows the same
321	      condition: what makes either pass run again is a changed state. A
322	      finding answered by argument alone leaves both passes nothing they
323	      have not already seen, and a round of findings answered by edits
324	      takes one rerun over the result rather than one per finding.
325	    - Push and create the pull request only after local verification and
326	      any required code review are complete.
327	    - Open a normal, ready-for-review pull request by default. Do not
328	      open draft pull requests unless the user explicitly asks for a
329	      draft.
330	
331	12. **Merge only clean, passing pull requests.** Merge only after GitHub
332	    reports a clean merge state and every configured check passes. Never
333	    bypass a failing or pending required check. Self-merges are allowed
334	    when these conditions are met.
335	    Use squash merge for short-lived development branches to keep `main`
336	    linear, then delete the merged branch.
337	
338	### Who runs which tests
339	
340	Steps 4 and 7 both run tests, and they are not running the same ones.
341	
342	**The main agent runs the test that is the subject of the change. The
343	`verifier` runs the rest of the battery.** Not everything else: the piped
344	plain-mode journey above and the 80x24/72x24 TUI check stay with whoever
345	made the change, since they are how you see your own work. The line does not
346	fall between unit tests and journeys; it falls on what the change is about.
347	A change to the pager makes `tests/tui.sh` the focused test and it belongs
348	in the loop, slow as it is. A change to `tuifmt.c` makes the compiled
349	`tuifmt` test the focused one, fast as it is, and leaves `tui` and the rest
350	to the `verifier` — including the golden recordings, which never pass `-t`
351	and so cannot see that file's panel formatters at all, whatever else in it
352	they reach.
353	
354	Step 4's loop cannot be delegated at all, and not because a sub-agent cannot
355	be trusted with it. Each failure decides the next edit, so the run and the
356	work are one act: what you would hand over is the whole of the task, and a
357	report arriving afterwards comes after the moment it was supposed to inform.
358	The entanglement is the reason, so a faster harness would not change it, and
359	neither would a focused test cheap enough to look worth handing over.
360	
361	What the `verifier` owns is everything the loop did not reach: the rest of
362	`ctest`, the full journey and golden battery, and the configurations the
363	main agent did not build — Release, `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, whatever the platform
364	adds. It decides that scope for itself: step 7 gives it the criterion, and
365	step 8 says the decision is the verifier's own. This says only that it
366	should not be asked to skip what the main agent happened to run, and that
367	the main agent should not pre-run the battery to save it the trouble.
368	Running the suite twice buys nothing and costs the whole of it: a full
369	`ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration. One caveat while it
370	stands: `verifier.md` does not yet ask for `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, which is
371	#125, so say so when invoking the pass.
372	
373	**Keep what reaches the main agent's context small.** That is the reason
374	this split is worth stating, and it is mechanical:
375	
376	- `ctest` prints no test output on a pass at all, and `--output-on-failure`
377	  costs nothing there while saving the second run a failure would otherwise
378	  need. `-R` scopes it to the test being worked on — anchor the pattern,
379	  since it is a regex: `-R tui` picks up `tuifmt` and `journey-tui` with it.
380	- The shell tests print one line on a pass, so they need no filtering. On a
381	  failure they print what broke and then dump the evidence behind it — a
382	  pane, a slice of game output, a diff, depending on the script — in that
383	  order, so it is the first lines that are worth reading and not the last:
384	  `2>&1 | head` keeps what broke, where `tail` keeps the dump and loses it.
385	- Grep a tmux pane for the string being asserted rather than capturing it
386	  whole. `capture-pane -p` is twenty-odd lines of screen and a TUI check
387	  makes many; capture the pane when the grep fails, which is when its
388	  content is worth reading.
389	
390	**The mutation proof in step 4 can be delegated**, unlike the loop in the
391	step it belongs to, and for the reason the loop cannot: it is one shot,
392	asked and answered, and what comes back is checkable. The break has a name,
393	and step 4 wants that name written down anyway, so a report that does not
394	give it is visibly incomplete.
395	
396	Not to one of the three review sub-agents — all of them are read-only by
397	definition, and a proof has to break something. A general-purpose sub-agent
398	is the one that can, working on a copy outside the repository, so nothing it
399	touches is tracked. Step 4 already asks for that copy where the proof runs
400	the game; ask for it whatever the proof breaks, because a sub-agent editing
401	the tree you are working in is a surprise nobody needs.
402	
403	What handing it off buys is context and not time, and the two do not track
404	each other: a proof that runs over three minutes is no cheaper delegated,
405	where one that prints twelve hundred lines is. So delegate when the failing
406	run would bury this context, which is a property of the test and worth
407	looking up rather than guessing — one line broken in `tui_refresh_panels()`
408	made `tui.sh` report 47 failures and 1209 lines of panes, `tournament.sh`
409	dumps up to 3000 bytes for every seed that fails, `golden.sh` a diff per
410	changed journey. Below that, and most proofs are below it — a broken `ctest
411	-R '^tuifmt$'` reports itself, with `--output-on-failure`, in a few dozen
412	lines, a broken `help` journey in sixty — there is nothing to bury, so keep
413	it.
414	
415	When you do hand it off, the sub-agent has to report what it broke precisely
416	enough for the main agent to write that down, since step 4 wants it in the
417	commit and in a comment beside the assertion.
418	
419	### The review sub-agents
420	
421	Steps 6-8 invoke Claude Code sub-agents defined in `.claude/agents/`:
422	`ui-review`, `verifier` and `code-review`. What matters is not the tool. It
423	is that the work is judged by a reader who did not write it, and who
424	reaches its conclusions from the diff rather than from a memory of having
425	intended something.
426	
427	Which of the three bind depends on what changed. `code-review` binds on
428	every commit, without exception — it is the gate step 8 describes.
429	`verifier` binds as well, with the scope step 7 already gives it: the
430	checks appropriate for the change, which for a file nothing compiles can
431	come down to a single test — the sub-agent still runs, even when what it
432	has to run is one test. `ui-review` binds when the change can alter what
433	the game shows a player or asks of them. This file, a test's plumbing and
434	CI configuration usually give it nothing to read; the build system does
435	the moment it changes what gets compiled in, since `-DSCORE`, `-DCAPTURE`,
436	`-DCLOAKING` and the `-DDEBUG` that Debug builds add all decide which
437	commands and messages the game has at all.
438	
439	When it is unclear whether a change reaches the player, run the pass. A
440	`ui-review` with nothing to say costs one pass; code that runs while the
441	game runs reaches the player whether the change meant it to or not, and a
442	refactor that preserves behavior is exactly where a lost line hides.
443	
444	Skipping it is a decision, not an omission. Say that it was skipped and
445	why — to `code-review` when invoking it, per step 8, and in the commit,
446	the pull request body and the summary of the work. The last three put it
447	on the record; the first is the one that reaches a reviewer with a
448	mandate to argue back, and reaches it before there is a commit to argue
449	about, which is why step 8 asks for it as well. An agent writing that
450	sentence about a change to the game's own output has skipped the wrong
451	pass.
452	
453	An agent that is not Claude Code is bound on the same terms, and cannot
454	satisfy a pass by reviewing its own work.
455	
456	- **A reviewer is a fresh session holding the reviewer's instructions, the
457	  change, and nothing else.** A sub-agent where the harness has them; a
458	  second non-interactive invocation of your own CLI — `codex exec` and its
459	  equivalents — where it does not. A new session reading the change cold
460	  satisfies this. The same session in a later turn does not.
461	- **Point at the definitions here rather than restating them.**
462	  `.claude/agents/ui-review.md`, `verifier.md` and `code-review.md` are the
463	  specifications. A per-tool definition should say to read the matching
464	  file and follow it, and carry only the wiring its own harness needs: the
465	  name, and that the reviewer reports findings and never edits. Copying the
466	  text is how three tools come to review three different things, which is
467	  the whole reason this file exists.
468	- **Keep the three names.** The workflow above, the commit history and the
469	  issue tracker all refer to them by name.
470	- **Land the definition as its own change,** on its own branch and commit,
471	  before the work it will review — not beside a feature, which step 10
472	  forbids and step 3 argues against. It belongs in the repository rather
473	  than in someone's local configuration for the same reason this file
474	  does: the next session in that tool then inherits a reviewer instead of
475	  improvising one, and an improvised reviewer drifts. That commit is also
476	  the one place self-review cannot be avoided, since step 8 cannot be
477	  satisfied by the commit that creates the reviewer. Say so in the commit,
478	  and disclose it as below.
479	- **Confirm the harness actually loads what you wrote.** A definition in a
480	  directory the tool never reads is inert, and from the outside it looks
481	  exactly like a step that was carried out.
482	- **Self-review is the last resort, not the default.** Taking it means
483	  saying which mechanism you looked for and why it was not there — or, for
484	  the commit that creates the reviewer, that it did not yet exist. Say it
485	  in the pull request body and in the summary of the work — in the summary
486	  alone when there is no pull request. A reviewer who shares the author's
487	  memory of what was intended is the one thing this section exists to prevent.
488	
489	### Answering a finding
490	
491	Steps 6, 7 and 8 hold their passes to one standard, in the same words:
492	fix every actionable finding, or resolve it explicitly. Two ways to
493	answer, and silence is neither.
494	
495	**Fixing** is the ordinary one, and most findings deserve it.
496	
497	**Resolving explicitly** is for the finding you judge wrong, or right
498	about something this change is not. Say what you think is true instead,
499	in the words you would use if you expected to be argued with.
500	
501	Where it goes depends on whether anything else is going to read the
502	change. A resolution alters no code, so it triggers no rerun: steps 6,
503	7 and 8 each condition theirs on a change, and step 11 forbids
504	repeating `code-review` over an unchanged worktree. So put it to the
505	next pass that runs anyway — step 8 already carries `ui-review` facts
506	into `code-review`, and a `verifier` finding you resolve is one
507	`code-review` should hear about. For a `code-review` finding resolved
508	without a change there is no next pass, and the record is the whole
509	of it.
510	
511	Either way it goes in the pull request body and in the summary of the
512	work — in the summary alone when there is no pull request, on the same
513	terms steps 3 and 9 already set. A resolution nobody can find
514	afterwards is the silence this rule exists to stop.
515	
516	What does not count: fixing something adjacent and calling the finding
517	handled, agreeing and then forgetting, or "I disagree" with no reason
518	under it. Filing an issue does not answer a finding about *this*
519	change — step 9 is explicit that filing is not resolving — but a
520	finding about code the change did not touch is answered by filing it
521	and saying so, which is step 9 working as intended rather than an
522	exception to it.

The workflow finished: 5 lenses → adversarial verification (12 of 30 findings survived) → synthesis. One correction to its "already filed" list: the CMakeLists timing finding is already covered by **#101** and **#127**, which weren't in the issue list I gave the agents.

## Verdict

The workflow itself is sound. The twelve steps, the "Who runs which tests" split, and "Answering a finding" compose without contradiction — the sequencing lens tried hardest to find a deadlock (step 6 rerun vs. step 11 "do not repeat", a `code-review` fix that changes player-visible output) and every candidate was refuted by text elsewhere in the file. The three sub-agents are the right three.

**What's broken is the seam between AGENTS.md and the three definition files.** The definitions are thinner than the rules they're meant to enforce. Every finding below is of the form "a required pass runs and looks at the wrong thing."

## Changes to make

**Blocker — `ui-review` cannot reach full-screen mode.** `.claude/agents/ui-review.md:35-38` gives one exercise method: "drive the affected behavior through `./build/sst`, scripting input via a pipe or heredoc." No `-t`, no pty. `grep -niE 'tui|curses|tmux|full-screen|80x24|72x24|pty' .claude/agents/ui-review.md` returns nothing. Its terminal-correctness criterion (`:54-56`) names "a plain 80-column terminal" only. So a change to `tui.c`/`tuifmt.c` — which is most of your recent history (58f5ea6, 8fbb4db, fef362c) — gets reviewed in the no-terminal fallback, and Output item 3 (`:69-70`) asks what *was* exercised but never what wasn't, so `code-review` can't see the miss. Add a step 4 under "How to review" pointing at the "TUI mode (`sst -t`)" section of AGENTS.md for the tmux rules, at 80x24 and 72x24; widen `:54` to cover both displays; make `:69-70` require naming which display was driven.

**Should-fix — no pass is briefed on the golden recordings.** `grep -rn 'golden\|fixture' .claude/agents/` is empty. Someone can run `golden.sh --update`, the verifier's `ctest` goes green, and `code-review` sees files under `tests/golden/` that look like an ordinary test edit — while the explanation AGENTS.md:89-93 demands goes into a commit message that doesn't exist yet at step 8. Add a "Golden recordings" bullet to code-review.md's "What to look for" treating an unexplained re-record as a blocker, and have verifier.md report `tests/golden/` in the diff under **What ran**.

**Should-fix — `verifier.md` builds Release and never uses it.** `:19-20` configures both trees; item 3 (`:27-29`) names no build dir and item 4 (`:31-33`) pins journeys to `./build-debug/sst`. Debug compiles in `-DDEBUG` (CMakeLists.txt:30-31), the shell tests take `$<CONFIG>` and branch on it (tests/tui.sh:1724, tests/journey.sh:177), and CI runs both. Since the main agent builds Debug, Release coverage exists only here — a `#ifdef DEBUG` regression reaches CI after a `Verdict: pass`.

**Should-fix — `code-review.md` never mentions the verifier.** `grep -c verifier .claude/agents/code-review.md` → 0.
